title: Acute Appendicitis
text: Acute appendicitis: clinical reference summary Findings. Acute appendicitis classically begins with periumbilical pain migrating to the right iliac fossa over 24 hours, worsened by movement, with anorexia, nausea, and low-grade fever. Localized tenderness at McBurney point with rebound and guarding is typical; Rovsing, psoas, and obturator signs add sensitivity. Young adults are most affected, although appendicitis occurs at any age. Differential diagnosis (ranked): (1) acute appendicitis; (2) mesenteric adenitis, often after viral illness in children; (3) Meckel diverticulitis; (4) Crohn terminal ileitis; (5) ectopic pregnancy in reproductive-age women, always test hCG; (6) ovarian torsion or ruptured cyst; (7) ureteric colic; (8) urinary tract infection. Recommended investigations. CBC for leukocytosis, CRP; urinalysis to exclude UTI/stone; beta-hCG in all women of childbearing age; ultrasound of the abdomen first, CT abdomen with contrast when ultrasound is inconclusive; Alvarado or AIR scores support risk stratification in documentation. Safety note: surgical decision-making is strictly human; the system only organizes findings, differentials, and investigations with citations.

title: Acute Myocardial Infarction
text: Acute myocardial infarction: clinical reference summary Findings. Acute myocardial infarction (AMI) usually presents with central crushing chest pain radiating to the jaw or left arm, sweating, nausea, and dyspnea, but presentations in women, elderly, and diabetic patients are frequently atypical: epigastric discomfort, isolated dyspnea, syncope, or fatigue. Ischemic-type chest discomfort plus elevated cardiac troponin confirms myocardial injury; ECG ST-segment changes classify STEMI versus NSTEMI. Differential diagnosis (ranked): (1) AMI; (2) stable angina, relieved by rest; (3) pulmonary embolism, with pleuritic pain and hypoxia; (4) aortic dissection, with tearing pain and pulse deficits; (5) pericarditis, positional pain with diffuse ST elevation; (6) musculoskeletal chest pain and GERD. Recommended investigations. Immediate 12-lead ECG (within 10 minutes) with serial tracings; high-sensitivity troponin at 0 and 1-3 hours; portable chest radiograph; pulse oximetry; echocardiography for wall-motion abnormalities and complications; after stabilization, risk stratification (GRACE score), coronary angiography, lipid profile, and HbA1c. Safety note: this reference supports observation report drafting only; emergency care decisions follow local STEMI protocols with physician review.

title: Chronic Kidney Disease
text: Chronic kidney disease: clinical reference summary Findings. Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is defined as abnormalities of kidney structure or function persisting for more than three months. It is usually asymptomatic until advanced stages, when anemia resistant to iron, hypertension, nocturia, pruritus, and edema appear. Diabetes and hypertension are the leading causes; eGFR stage 1-5 classification with A1-A3 albuminuria stage quantifies risk of progression. Differential diagnosis (ranked for acute-on-chronic presentations): (1) CKD progression; (2) prerenal acute kidney injury from dehydration, NSAIDs, sepsis; (3) acute interstitial nephritis, medication allergic features; (4) obstructive uropathy with hydronephrosis; (5) rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with active urinary sediment. Recommended investigations. Serum creatinine with eGFR trend, urine albumin-creatinine ratio, urinalysis for protein and sediment; renal ultrasound for size and obstruction; CBC, calcium, phosphate, vitamin D, PTH in advanced stage; HbA1c and lipid profile if diabetic. Avoid nephrotoxins; review all medications including metformin dose relevance for eGFR. Traceability note: staging formulas and referral thresholds should cite retrieved guideline passages such as KDIGO summaries rather than model memory.

title: Community Acquired Pneumonia
text: Community-acquired pneumonia: clinical reference summary Findings. Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) presents with acute-onset fever, productive cough, dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and focal crackles or bronchial breathing on auscultation. In older adults, confusion and fatigue may dominate without classic fever. CURB-65 (confusion, urea >7 mmol/L, respiratory rate >=30, blood pressure <90/60, age >=65) stratifies severity and guides site of care. Differential diagnosis (ranked): (1) CAP (bacterial, often Streptococcus pneumoniae); (2) atypical pneumonia (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella) with prodrome, dry cough, and GI symptoms; (3) pulmonary tuberculosis, especially with night sweats, weight loss, and prolonged symptoms; (4) acute bronchitis, typically without focal lung findings; (5) pulmonary embolism when breathlessness is disproportionate; (6) heart failure mimicking pneumonia in the elderly. Recommended investigations. Chest radiograph for consolidation; CBC, CRP, blood urea; pulse oximetry; sputum Gram stain and culture, blood cultures if septic; urinary Legionella and pneumococcal antigens in severe cases; COVID-19 and influenza PCR in season; D-dimer/CTPA if PE suspected. Biomarkers such as procalcitonin can help de-escalate antibiotics. Traceability note: claims about antimicrobial therapy should cite current guideline passages retrieved from the knowledge base rather than restating memorized protocols.

title: Hyperthyroidism Graves
text: Hyperthyroidism (Graves disease): clinical reference summary Findings. Hyperthyroidism presents with weight loss despite normal appetite, heat intolerance, palpitations, tremor, anxiety, insomnia, sweating, and fatigue. Graves disease adds diffuse smooth goiter, ophthalmopathy (proptosis, diplopia), and pretibial myxedema; brisk reflexes and wide pulse pressure are common examination findings. Thyrotoxic crisis is a life-threatening decompensation with fever and delirium. Differential diagnosis (ranked): (1) Graves disease, suppressed TSH with elevated free T4/T3 and TSH-receptor antibodies; (2) toxic multinodular goiter, hot nodules on scan; (3) toxic adenoma; (4) thyroiditis, transient thyrotoxicosis with low radioiodine uptake; (5) exogenous hormone or iodine intake; (6) factitious thyroid hormone use. Recommended investigations. First-line TSH, free T4, free T3; TSH-receptor antibodies (TRAb) to confirm Graves; thyroid ultrasound and radioiodine uptake scan when etiology is unclear; ECG for atrial fibrillation; CBC and LFTs at baseline before antithyroid therapy consultation. Traceability note: any statement on antithyroid drug choice, dosing, or radioiodine must attach a retrieved guideline citation; otherwise the claim is flagged and suppressed.

title: Hypothyroidism
text: Hypothyroidism: clinical reference summary Findings. Hypothyroidism produces insidious fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, dry skin, hair loss, bradycardia, and delayed relaxation of ankle reflexes. In women, menstrual irregularity and subfertility are common. The most frequent cause worldwide is iodine deficiency and in iodine-sufficient regions, autoimmune (Hashimoto) thyroiditis confirmed by positive anti-TPO antibodies and a diffuse firm goiter. Differential diagnosis (ranked): (1) primary hypothyroidism, high TSH with low free T4; (2) subclinical hypothyroidism, high TSH with normal T4; (3) secondary (central) hypothyroidism, low or normal TSH with low free T4, suspect pituitary disease; (4) non-thyroidal illness syndrome in severe systemic illness; (5) depression, anemia mimickers producing overlapping fatigue. Recommended investigations. TSH and free T4 are first-line; anti-TPO antibodies to establish autoimmune etiology; lipid profile (commonly elevated), CBC for anemia, CK for myopathy; morning cortisol if central hypothyroidism suspected; gluten serology for associated celiac disease when indicated. Traceability note: levothyroxine dosing and follow-up intervals must cite retrieved guideline passages; models must not generate treatment prescriptions without evidence references.

title: Iron Deficiency Anemia
text: Iron deficiency anemia: clinical reference summary Findings. Iron deficiency anemia typically presents with fatigue, exertional dyspnea, pallor, headache, and sometimes pica or glossitis. Common causes in adults include chronic blood loss (menorrhagia, gastrointestinal bleeding) and inadequate dietary intake; in vegetarian or vegan diets, non-heme iron bioavailability is low. Microcytic anemia (low MCV, high RDW) with low serum ferritin (<30 ug/L) and low transferrin saturation is diagnostic. Serum ferritin is the single most useful test but rises with inflammation, so concomitant CRP helps interpretation. Differential diagnosis (ranked by typical relevance for microcytic anemia): (1) iron deficiency anemia; (2) anemia of chronic disease/inflammation; (3) thalassemia trait, suggested by very low MCV with normal or high RDW and a Mentzer index (MCV/RBC) < 13; (4) sideroblastic anemia (rare, elderly). Recommended investigations. Complete blood count with reticulocytes; serum iron studies (ferritin, transferrin saturation, TIBC); CRP; celiac serology if refractory; in men and in postmenopausal women, endoscopy and colonoscopy to exclude occult GI malignancy. Response to oral iron (hemoglobin rise of 10-20 g/L in 4 weeks) confirms the diagnosis. Traceability note: every claim should be anchored to a retrieved passage from PubMed abstracts or NCBI Bookshelf chapter sources in the knowledge base.

title: Ischemic Stroke
text: Ischemic stroke: clinical reference summary Findings. Ischemic stroke presents with sudden focal neurological deficit: unilateral weakness or numbness, facial droop, dysarthria or aphasia, visual field loss, or ataxia. Onset-to-assessment time is critical because thrombolysis is typically within 4.5 hours and thrombectomy windows extend to 24 hours in selected large-vessel occlusions. The FAST/BE-FAST screens guide prehospital recognition. Chronic risk factors include atrial fibrillation, hypertension, diabetes, smoking, and prior stroke. Differential diagnosis (ranked): (1) ischemic stroke; (2) transient ischemic attack, with complete resolution; (3) intracerebral hemorrhage, headache and depressed consciousness favor it; (4) hypoglycemia, always excluded at bedside; (5) seizure with Todd palsy; (6) complex migraine with aura. Recommended investigations. Emergent non-contrast CT head to exclude hemorrhage; glucose at point of care; ECG for atrial fibrillation; CT angiography for large-vessel occlusion if thrombectomy considered; laboratory workup (CBC, coagulation, electrolytes); after stabilization, echocardiography, carotid imaging, and prolonged rhythm monitoring. Traceability note: eligibility criteria for reperfusion therapies are time sensitive and should always be verified against retrieved current-guideline evidence.

title: Pulmonary Tuberculosis
text: Pulmonary tuberculosis: clinical reference summary Findings. Pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) presents classically with more than two weeks of productive cough, night sweats, low-grade evening fever, weight loss, anorexia, and hemoptysis in advanced disease. Host risk factors include immunosuppression, diabetes, malnutrition, and close TB contact. In India, where the project context is set, universal drug susceptibility testing at diagnosis is recommended practice. Differential diagnosis (ranked): (1) pulmonary tuberculosis; (2) community-acquired bacterial pneumonia; (3) lung malignancy, especially in older smokers; (4) fungal infections (histoplasmosis, aspergillosis); (5) sarcoidosis; (6) bronchiectasis. Recommended investigations. Sputum smear for acid-fast bacilli plus Xpert MTB/RIF (NAAT) is the recommended first diagnostic test; chest radiograph with cavitation, upper-lobe infiltrates, and hilar lymphadenopathy; tuberculin skin test or IGRA for latent infection assessment; HIV test for all; CBC, LFTs before therapy. Bronchoscopy for sputum-negative cases with high suspicion. Public health note: PTB is a notifiable disease in India; diagnosis triggers contact tracing and standardized treatment under national program supervision. The CDSS must cite notified-guideline retrieval passages for any therapeutic statement.

title: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
text: Type 2 diabetes mellitus: clinical reference summary Findings. Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) often presents with polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, recurrent infections, blurred vision, or may be asymptomatic and found on screening. Risk factors include obesity, sedentary lifestyle, family history, and South Asian, African, or Hispanic ethnicity. Diagnostic criteria via fasting plasma glucose >= 126 mg/dL, 2-hour OGTT >= 200 mg/dL, HbA1c >= 6.5%, or random glucose >= 200 mg/dL with classic symptoms, each confirmed by repeat testing unless unequivocal hyperglycemia. Differential diagnosis (ranked): (1) T2DM; (2) type 1/LADA suggested by low BMI, ketosis, younger age, low C-peptide with autoimmune antibodies; (3) secondary diabetes from steroids, pancreatitis, hemochromatosis; (4) stress hyperglycemia during acute illness; (5) gestational diabetes in pregnancy. Recommended investigations. First-line HbA1c, fasting glucose profile; baseline urine albumin-creatinine ratio, serum creatinine/eGFR, lipid panel, LFTs; diabetic retinal screening; foot inspection with monofilament testing; ECG. Monitor treatment with periodic HbA1c. Safety note: insulin and medication selection must be left to the treating clinician; the system's role is grounded observation summaries, not prescriptions.
